column1: # English orthographic grapheme classes — the vowel/consonant partition of the
# 26 basic-Latin letters used by English spelling, plus the ONE letter whose
# class is genuinely dual.
# Why this table exists: the morphological GENERATION rules
# (`morphology::english::generation`) and the irregular-table oracle
# (`morphology::english::irregular`) each carried their own private
#     fn is_vowel(c: char) -> bool { matches!(c, 'a'|'e'|'i'|'o'|'u') }
# — the English vowel inventory hardcoded as a Rust match arm, duplicated in
# two files, with `y`'s dual status scattered alongside it as ad-hoc
# `|| c == 'y'` tests. The RULES those functions implement are cited (Quirk
# et al. 1985 §3, §3.21; Spencer 1991 §5.2) but the ALPHABET they range over
# was not loaded from anywhere. This table is that alphabet, loaded and cited,
# so the rules query a vocabulary instead of a literal.
# The vowel/consonant split of the Latin alphabet as used for English is not a
# Unicode property — the UCD classifies these code points only as
# General_Category=Ll/Lu (letters); it says nothing about vowel-hood, which is
# a language-specific orthographic fact. So this is an AUTHORED table from the
# descriptive literature, not a UCD derivation.
# Sources:
#   Carney, Edward (1994). *A Survey of English Spelling*. London: Routledge.
#     The standard descriptive survey of English orthography. Ch. 1 sets out
#     the basic-Latin letter inventory used by English and its division into
#     vowel letters <a, e, i, o, u> and consonant letters, and treats <y> as
#     the letter with dual vowel/consonant function.
#   Quirk, Randolph; Greenbaum, Sidney; Leech, Geoffrey; Svartvik, Jan (1985).
#     *A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language*. London: Longman.
#     §3.21 states the orthographic plural rule in terms of a *consonant*
#     before a final <y> ("baby" -> "babies", but "boy" -> "boys" because the
#     <y> follows a vowel) — i.e. the rule is stated over exactly this
#     partition, and depends on <y> itself patterning as a vowel in "boy".
# On <y> (class = Dual): <y> spells a consonant word-initially and
# syllable-initially ("yes", "beyond") and a vowel elsewhere ("baby",
# "rhythm", "boy"). Both cited sources treat it as dual rather than assigning
# it to one class. The consuming code must therefore ask which ROLE it is
# playing rather than asking a boolean "is it a vowel", and the two roles are
# separated in the two query methods on the loaded vocabulary — the
# syllable-peak count treats <y> as a vowel (so "rhythm" has a peak), while
# the consonant-before-final-<y> test treats a preceding <y> as NOT a
# consonant (so "boy" -> "boys"). Those are the two behaviours the previous
# hardcoded `is_vowel` + `|| c == 'y'` pair implemented by hand.
# Column format:
#   letter  class   note
# where class is one of: Vowel | Consonant | Dual
letter
a
e
i
o
u
y
